title: The gut as a neuroimmune hub
objective: Explain why the gut wall is a prime site of neuroimmune interaction.

steps.title: Nerves and immune cells, side by side
steps.body: The gut faces trillions of microbes across a thin wall, so it packs immune cells densely into the **[[lamina propria]]** — right where sensory ([[DRG]] and vagal) endings also run. Nerves and immune cells share the same real estate, making the gut a natural neuroimmune hub.

steps.prompt: Why is the gut especially rich in neuroimmune interaction?
options: Sensory endings and dense immune cells share the wall, facing the microbiota
The gut wall is thick enough that nerves and immune cells rarely meet
Nerves and immune cells are kept apart in totally separate organs there
The gut contains no sensory neurons whatsoever, only immune cells present
steps.explanation: A thin, heavily-colonized surface means immune cells and sensory endings are packed together in the wall — ideal conditions for them to signal to each other.

variants.setup: The gut faces a huge microbial load across a thin wall.
options: Dense immune cells next to sensory endings
Total separation of nerves and immune cells
A wall with no sensory innervation
variants.reveal: The thin, colonized wall packs immune cells and nerve endings together.

steps.title: The lab's front line
steps.body: This is exactly where the lab works: mapping which [[DRG]] sensory subtypes sit among which immune and epithelial cells in the colon wall — the cellular stage for everything in this track.

sources.note: DRG afferents in the colon wall, among lamina-propria immune cells.

sources.citation: Wallrapp A & Chiu IM, 2024, Annu Rev Immunol
